2027-05-15.title: Saturday of the Seventh Week of Easter
readings: He lived there two whole years and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God
The upright shall behold his face (or: Alleluia)
This is the disciple who is testifying to these things and has written them, and his testimony is true
2027-05-15.alt: Easter weekday of the seventh week (Year I), in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost. In India the Ascension was celebrated on Sunday 9 May. Until Pentecost one of the Prefaces of the Ascension or of Easter is said, the paschal candle burns beside the ambo, and the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus. Many parishes pray the novena to the Holy Spirit in these days, as the apostles prayed with Mary in the upper room. Liturgical colour: white. This is the last weekday of the Easter season. In the evening the Vigil Mass of Pentecost is celebrated, in its simple form or as an extended vigil with several readings (Genesis 11:1–9; Exodus 19; Ezekiel 37:1–14; Joel 2:28–32, numbered 3:1–5 in some Bibles; Romans 8:22–27; John 7:37–39). Today both the Acts of the Apostles and the Gospel of John, read through the fifty days, come to their last page.
2027-05-15.verse: Jesus said to him, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? Follow me!”
theo: For fifty days the Church has read the Acts of the Apostles, from the Ascension at Jerusalem to the shipwreck at Malta. Today we reach the last page, and it ends in Rome. Paul has arrived as a prisoner, but a strange kind of prisoner: “Paul was allowed to live by himself, with the soldier who was guarding him.” Three days later he calls together the leaders of the Jewish community of Rome. He speaks to them as “brothers,” and he insists that he has “done nothing against our people or the customs of our ancestors,” and that he has “no charge to bring against my nation.” Then he says why he wears a chain: “it is for the sake of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.” Paul never stopped being a son of Israel; the risen Messiah is, for him, the fulfilment of Israel's own hope, not its rejection. And the book ends with a picture rather than a conclusion: “He lived there two whole years at his own expense and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.” Luke does not tell us how Paul's trial ended, or how he died. The last word of Acts in Greek is akōlytōs, “without hindrance.” The apostle is in chains, but the word of God is not. The story of the Church is left open, for us to continue. The Psalm gives the reason for that boldness: “The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord's throne is in heaven,” and “the upright shall behold his face.”

The Gospel of John ends in the same open way. On the shore of the lake the risen Jesus has just asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?” and told him how he would one day glorify God by his death. Peter turns, sees the beloved disciple following them, and asks a very human question: “Lord, what about him?” Jesus answers gently but firmly: “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? Follow me!” Each disciple has his own road. Peter will die a martyr; John, tradition tells us, will live long and die in peace. Comparison is a waste of time; what matters is following. Then the evangelist steps forward: “This is the disciple who is testifying to these things and has written them, and we know that his testimony is true.” The Gospel rests on the witness of one who reclined next to Jesus at the supper and stood at the foot of the cross with Mary. And it ends with a smile: “if every one of them were written down, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.” Tonight, at the Vigil of Pentecost, the Church will hear Jesus cry out: “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me.” The last weekday of Easter ends where the novena began, in the upper room, waiting with Mary for the gift that will write the rest of the story in us.
outline: Ask: how would you feel if your favourite book ended in the middle of a sentence?
Point 1 · For the hope of Israel
Paul in chains in Rome, still a son of his people.
The open ending of Acts and the word that cannot be chained.
Point 3 · What is that to you? Follow me!
Each disciple's own road, and the true witness of John.
live: When you catch yourself comparing your life with someone else's today, say quietly: what is that to me? Lord, I will follow you.
Tonight or tomorrow morning, spend ten minutes in silence and ask the Holy Spirit for the one gift you need most. If you can, join the Vigil of Pentecost in your parish.
2027-05-15.prayer: Lord Jesus, you told Peter: What is that to you? Follow me! Deliver us from comparing ourselves with others, and give us the grace to follow you on the road you have chosen for each of us. Like Paul in Rome, let us proclaim your kingdom with boldness, even when we are bound; like the beloved disciple, let us bear true witness to what we have seen of your love. As Easter draws to its close, we wait with Mary and the apostles: send us your Holy Spirit, the Advocate, the giver of life. Come, Holy Spirit. Amen.
altar: Paul in Rome “welcomed all who came to him.” The risen Lord does the same at every altar: whoever comes to him in faith he will never drive away. Tonight's Vigil and tomorrow's Mass of Pentecost will celebrate the Spirit who, at every Eucharist, is called down upon the gifts so that they become the Body and Blood of Christ, and upon us so that we become one body in him.

quick: Acts ends in Rome: Paul, a prisoner, welcomes all who come and proclaims the kingdom with boldness and without hindrance.
He tells the Jewish leaders of Rome that he is bound for the sake of the hope of Israel.
John's Gospel ends: Jesus tells Peter not to worry about the beloved disciple but to follow him; the Gospel rests on that disciple's true witness.
2027-05-15.action: Each time you compare yourself with someone today, turn it into a prayer: Lord, I will follow you.
2027-05-15.question: Am I so busy watching other people's roads that I forget to follow Jesus on mine?

family.explain: After Jesus rose, Peter asked him about John: Lord, what about him? Jesus said: don't worry about him. You follow me! Jesus has a special path for each one of us. Today is the last ordinary day of Easter. Tomorrow is Pentecost, the birthday of the Church, when the Holy Spirit came!
family.intention: We pray for our Church as Pentecost comes, and for prisoners and all who are in chains.
family.ask: Ask: “Do we sometimes compare ourselves with our brothers, sisters or friends? How can we stop?” Then pray together: Come, Holy Spirit!

illus: Two sisters in a Thrissur family were always being compared: one was good at mathematics, the other at music. Their grandmother kept a small framed card on the wall with the words of John 21:22: What is that to you? Follow me! When they quarrelled about who was better, she would point at the card and say: God has not given you the same road; he has given you the same Lord. Years later one became a nurse and the other a music teacher, and both say that card taught them to stop competing and start following.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you call each of us by name and say: Follow me! Give us your Spirit, so that we may follow you with boldness and joy. Amen.
share: It is for the sake of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain (Acts 28:20). What hope am I ready to suffer for?
Proclaiming the kingdom of God … with all boldness and without hindrance (Acts 28:31). What stops me from speaking about Jesus?
What is that to you? Follow me! (John 21:22). Whom do I compare myself with, and what does Jesus say to me about it?
pm.resp: The upright shall behold his face.
interc: For the Church on the eve of Pentecost, that she may be renewed by the Holy Spirit.
For prisoners, especially those imprisoned for their faith, that the word of God may not be chained in them.
For the Jewish people, the first to hear the word of God, that they may be blessed in faithfulness to his covenant.
For all who feel they are not as gifted as others, that they may find joy in their own road.
For our group, that we may be found praying together with Mary when the Holy Spirit comes.
pm.close: Father, at the close of the Easter season we wait for the promise of your Son. Pour out your Spirit on us, so that we may follow Christ and bear true witness to him. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today we come to the last page of two books. Since Easter we have been reading the Acts of the Apostles and the Gospel of John. Both end today, and both end in a surprising way: not with a full stop, but with an open door.

Acts ends in Rome. Paul is a prisoner, chained to a soldier, but he is not silent. He calls the Jewish leaders of the city his brothers, and he tells them: it is for the sake of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain (Acts 28:20). Then for two whole years he welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance (Acts 28:31). We do not hear how his trial ended. Luke leaves the story open, because it is not finished. We are the next chapter.

John's Gospel ends on the shore of the lake. Peter has just been told how he would die, and he looks at John and asks: Lord, what about him? How often we do the same! Why does he have it easier? Why did she get that gift and not me? Jesus answers: what is that to you? Follow me! (John 21:22). Each of us has a road. Our task is not to measure the roads of others, but to walk our own behind Jesus.

Tonight, at the Vigil of Pentecost, the Church will pray with the apostles and with Mary for the gift of the Holy Spirit. Let us bring to that prayer our chains and our comparisons. The Spirit who made Paul bold in chains and made John a true witness will make us bold and true as well. The world could not contain all the books about Jesus; let the Holy Spirit write a few more lines in our lives. Come, Holy Spirit. Amen.
kids: Children, today two books in the Bible come to their last page. In the first one, St Paul is a prisoner in Rome, but he still tells everyone about Jesus. In the second, Peter asks Jesus: what about John? And Jesus says: don't worry about him, you follow me! Jesus has a special path just for you. Tomorrow is Pentecost, the birthday of the Church! Let us say: Come, Holy Spirit!

intro: Theme: “What is that to you? Follow me!”
The last page of Acts and the last page of John: an apostle unchained in spirit, and a disciple called to follow on his own road.

sub: The Messiah, fulfilment of Israel's hope.
q: For surely I know the plans I have for you, says the Lord, plans for your welfare and not for harm, to give you a future with hope.
For this reason therefore I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is for the sake of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.
points.apply: Pray this week for the Jewish people and for good relations between Christians and Jews, remembering that our hope was first theirs.

sub: Two whole years in a rented house.
The word that cannot be chained.
q: So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and succeed in the thing for which I sent it.
proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.
points.apply: Welcome one person into your home or your time this week, and let them see your faith.

points.h: What is that to you? Follow me!
sub: A true witness who has written.
q: Where you go, I will go; where you lodge, I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your God my God.
Jesus said to him, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? Follow me!”
points.apply: Name one person you often compare yourself with, and pray for them by name each day until next Sunday.

concl: Acts and John both end with an open door: the story of Christ's witnesses is not finished.
The Spirit who comes at Pentecost will write the next lines in us, if we follow Jesus on our own road and bear true witness.
2027-05-15.resolve: Join the Vigil of Pentecost or pray tonight for the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and stop comparing; follow.
